\chapter{The Roman Calendar}
\label{ch:monate-roemisch}
\hlchaptermodality{13}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the first six German months and say why every one of the twelve came from Latin.}

The unit is German's own -- der Monat IS der Mond, one turn of it, exactly as English month is moon. The twelve names inside it are Latin, taken whole with the calendar that ordered them. The chapter walks the first six and stops on the one that arrived twice: Maerz is Mars by name, and Dienstag is the same god by translation, because German already had a week to map onto and no twelve-month calendar at all.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[der Monat]{der Monat — \textquotedblleft{}the month\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C09-monate}



\begin{quote}
Twelve names are coming, and every one of them is Latin. The word that holds them is not.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: der Monat}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{der Monat} — \textquotedblleft{}the month.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Say \emph{Mond} and then \emph{Monat} and you have heard the whole etymology. They are the same word: a month is a \textbf{moon}, one turn of it. English does this too — \emph{moon} and \emph{month} — and neither language got the idea from the other, because both inherited it.

The plural is \emph{die Monate}, \textquotedblleft{}the months,\textquotedblright{} and it is the form the chapter title uses.

\begin{culture}
Here is the shape of the next two chapters, in one sentence.

The \textbf{unit} is German's own, inherited, older than any calendar: a moon. The \textbf{names} for the twelve are borrowed whole from Rome, along with the calendar that ordered them.

You met that division in the numbers chapter, where the counting words stayed home and the month names came in. This is where you meet the month names.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}der Mond, der Monat\textquotedblright{}
  \item the English pair — \textquotedblleft{}moon, month\textquotedblright{}
  \item singular and plural — \textquotedblleft{}der Monat, die Monate\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}der Mond, der Monat.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}the month.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Der Monat}.) What German word is hiding in it? (\emph{\textbf{Mond}}, the moon.) Is \emph{Monat} borrowed? (\textbf{No} — it is inherited.) And the twelve names about to arrive? (\textbf{Latin}, all of them.) Next: the first one.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[der Januar]{der Januar — \textquotedblleft{}January\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C09-januar}



\begin{quote}
The first of the twelve borrowed names, and it is a doorway.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: der Januar}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{der Januar} — \textquotedblleft{}January.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Latin \emph{Januarius}, the month of \textbf{Janus} — the Roman god of doors, gateways and beginnings, shown with two faces because a doorway looks both ways at once.

A first month is exactly that: the year behind you and the year ahead, seen from the same spot.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{j-as-y} — German \emph{j} is English \emph{y}. \emph{Januar} begins \textbf{ya-}, not \textbf{ja-}.
  \item \texttt{vowel-a-long} — and the \emph{a} that follows is long and open.
\end{itemize}

\emph{YA-nu-ar}, with the weight on the first syllable.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}der Januar\textquotedblright{} — YA-nu-ar
  \item the god in it — \textquotedblleft{}Janus\textquotedblright{}
  \item what a first month is — \textquotedblleft{}a door that looks both ways\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}der Januar.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}January.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Der Januar}.) How does the \emph{j} sound? (\textbf{Like an English} \emph{y}.) Which god? (\textbf{Janus}, of doorways.) Why two faces? (\textbf{A doorway looks both ways}.) Next: a month named for a washing.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[der Februar]{der Februar — \textquotedblleft{}February\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C09-februar}



\begin{quote}
The second month, and the odd one out among the twelve.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: der Februar}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{der Februar} — \textquotedblleft{}February.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Latin \emph{Februarius}, from the \emph{\textbf{Februa}} — a purification festival the Romans held at that point in the year, a washing-clean before the new season.

Every other month you will meet is named for a \textbf{god}, an \textbf{emperor}, or a \textbf{number}. This one is named for something people \emph{did}.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{vowel-e-german} — the \emph{e} of \emph{Fe-} is a clear short \emph{e}, not the English \emph{feb}'s flat vowel.
  \item \texttt{r-final} — and the ending is the same soft closing \emph{r} you met on \emph{Uhr}.
\end{itemize}

\emph{FAY-bru-ar}, four beats, weight on the first.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}der Februar\textquotedblright{} — FAY-bru-ar
  \item the first two in order — \textquotedblleft{}Januar, Februar\textquotedblright{}
  \item what it is named for — \textquotedblleft{}a washing-clean\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Januar, Februar.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}February.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Der Februar}.) Is it named for a god? (\textbf{No} — for a \textbf{festival}, the \emph{Februa}.) Say the first two months together. (\textbf{Januar, Februar}.) Next: a god you have already met, arriving a second time.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[der März]{der März — \textquotedblleft{}March\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C09-maerz}



\begin{quote}
You already know something about this month from the numbers chapter, though not its name.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: der März}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{der März} — \textquotedblleft{}March.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Latin \emph{Martius}, the month of \textbf{Mars}, the war-god. Campaigning weather began here, and so did the Roman year.

That second fact is the one you have already been given: the Roman year opened here. Four of the twelve names still count from this month, and you will meet them in the next chapter.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{vowel-ae} — \emph{ä} is a bright open \emph{e}, close to English \emph{bed}. Not the \emph{ar} of English \emph{March}.
  \item \texttt{tz-affricate} — and \emph{-rz} ends on a \textbf{ts}, so the word closes \emph{merts}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}der März\textquotedblright{} — merts
  \item the god — \textquotedblleft{}Mars\textquotedblright{}
  \item three in order — \textquotedblleft{}Januar, Februar, März\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}der März.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}March.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Der März}.) How does \emph{-rz} end? (\textbf{On a} \emph{ts}.) Which god? (\textbf{Mars}.) Where did the Roman year begin? (\textbf{Here, in March}.) Next: the same god, under a name you already own.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[März und Dienstag]{März and Dienstag}

\label{lesson:GE-C09-maerz-mars}



\begin{quote}
Two German words you now own. They come from the same god, and neither of them looks like the other.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Mars} entered German \textbf{twice}, and by two different routes.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the route} & \textbf{what German got} & \textbf{result} \\
\midrule
his \textbf{name}, borrowed whole & Latin \emph{Martius} & \emph{März} \\
his \textbf{job}, given to Tiw & Germanic \emph{Tiwaz} & \emph{Dienstag} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

When the Romans met the Germanic gods, they matched them up by what they did: the war-god here answers the war-god there. Tuesday was Mars's day, so it became Tiw's day, and it still is — in German \emph{Dienstag}, in English \textbf{Tuesday}.

The month got no such treatment. Nobody translated \emph{Martius}; German took it as it stood.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
The difference is worth holding onto, because it is the whole chapter in one example.

The \textbf{week} was a thing Germanic speakers already had, so when the Roman scheme arrived they mapped it onto their own gods and kept their own words. The \textbf{calendar of twelve months} was not; it came in as an administrative object, name-plates and all, and German took the name-plates.

Same god, same century, two outcomes — decided by whether German already had something to put in the slot.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}März, Dienstag\textquotedblright{}
  \item what each did with the god — \textquotedblleft{}took his name; took his job\textquotedblright{}
  \item the reason — \textquotedblleft{}German had a week already; it had no twelve months\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}März and Dienstag — one god, two doors.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two German words carry Mars? (\emph{\textbf{März}} \textbf{and} \emph{\textbf{Dienstag}}.) Which took his name? (\emph{\textbf{März}}.) Which took his job? (\emph{\textbf{Dienstag}}, through \textbf{Tiw}.) Why did the week get translated and the calendar not? (\textbf{German already had a week}.) Next: a month that may be named for an opening.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[der April]{der April — \textquotedblleft{}April\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C09-april}



\begin{quote}
Three months in and every name has had an owner. This one does not.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: der April}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{der April} — \textquotedblleft{}April.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Latin \emph{Aprilis}. Where that came from is genuinely unsettled — the Romans of the classical period were already guessing. The oldest and best guess is \emph{aperire}, \textquotedblleft{}to open,\textquotedblright{} for the month when things do.

Say it aloud and notice where the weight sits: German puts it on the \textbf{second} syllable, \emph{a-PRIL}, where English puts it on the first.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{r-uvular} — the \emph{r} in \emph{-pril} is made at the back of the throat, closer to a soft scrape than an English roll.
  \item \texttt{i-short} — and the \emph{i} is short and bright: \emph{pril}, not \emph{preel}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}der April\textquotedblright{} — a-PRIL, weight at the back
  \item the guess — \textquotedblleft{}aperire, to open\textquotedblright{}
  \item four in order — \textquotedblleft{}Januar, Februar, März, April\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}der April.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}April.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Der April}.) Which syllable carries the weight? (\textbf{The second} — a-PRIL.) Who is it named for? (\textbf{Nobody knows} — perhaps \emph{aperire}, \textquotedblleft{}to open\textquotedblright{}.) Next: a goddess of growing things.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[der Mai]{der Mai — \textquotedblleft{}May\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C09-mai}



\begin{quote}
One syllable, and its vowel is one you were given for a number.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: der Mai}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{der Mai} — \textquotedblleft{}May.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Latin \emph{Maius}, the month of \textbf{Maia} — a goddess of growth and increase, which is a reasonable thing to call the month when everything is putting on size.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{ai-as-eye} — \emph{ai} is the vowel of English \textbf{eye}.
\end{itemize}

You already have that vowel under its commoner German spelling, \emph{ei}, from the numbers. German writes the same sound two ways, and \emph{Mai} is the rarer one: \emph{ei} and \emph{ai} both say \textbf{eye}.

So \emph{Mai} rhymes with English \emph{my}.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}der Mai\textquotedblright{} — rhymes with \textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{}
  \item the goddess — \textquotedblleft{}Maia, of growing things\textquotedblright{}
  \item five in order — \textquotedblleft{}Januar, Februar, März, April, Mai\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}der Mai.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}May.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Der Mai}.) What does \emph{ai} sound like? (\textbf{English} \emph{eye}.) Which other spelling gives that sound? (\emph{\textbf{Ei}}.) Which goddess? (\textbf{Maia}.) Next: the queen of the gods.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[der Juni]{der Juni — \textquotedblleft{}June\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C09-juni}



\begin{quote}
Its first letter behaves exactly as the first month's did.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: der Juni}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{der Juni} — \textquotedblleft{}June.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Latin \emph{Junius}, the month of \textbf{Juno} — Jupiter's queen, and the goddess Romans married under, which is why June weddings are a Roman habit that never stopped.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{j-as-y} — the same \emph{j} as \emph{Januar}: English \emph{y}. \emph{YOO-ni}, never \emph{joon}.
  \item \texttt{ie-long-ee} — and the final \emph{i} is a long \emph{ee}.
\end{itemize}

Spoken German often lengthens this one to \emph{Juno} when a date has to be clear over the phone, because the month after it sounds far too close. That is a real habit, not something you have to learn now.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}der Juni\textquotedblright{} — YOO-nee
  \item the goddess — \textquotedblleft{}Juno\textquotedblright{}
  \item six in order — \textquotedblleft{}Januar, Februar, März, April, Mai, Juni\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}der Juni.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}June.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Der Juni}.) How does the \emph{j} sound? (\textbf{Like English} \emph{y}.) Which other month opens the same way? (\emph{\textbf{Januar}}.) Which goddess? (\textbf{Juno}.) Next: all six, said through.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — half a Roman year}

\label{lesson:GE-C09-monate-praxis}



\begin{quote}
No new words. Six names and the container they sit in.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: what German owns and what it bought}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what} & \textbf{German} & \textbf{where from} \\
\midrule
the \textbf{unit} & \emph{der Monat} & inherited — it is \emph{der Mond} \\
the \textbf{names} & \emph{Januar … Juni} & Latin, taken whole \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

One line, and it is the chapter. German had a moon and needed no help naming the span. It had no twelve-month calendar, so when one arrived it took the labels that came with it.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
Notice what the six names are \emph{for}, because they are not one kind of thing:

\emph{ \emph{\textbf{Januar}} — a god, \textbf{Janus} of doorways. } \emph{\textbf{Februar}} — not a god at all, but a \textbf{festival}, the \emph{Februa}. \emph{ \emph{\textbf{März}} — a god, \textbf{Mars}, who is also in }Dienstag\emph{ under another name. } \emph{\textbf{April}} — unknown, and unknown already in Rome. \emph{ \emph{\textbf{Mai}} — a goddess, \textbf{Maia} of growth. } \emph{\textbf{Juni}} — a goddess, \textbf{Juno}, queen of the gods.

Four deities, one ritual, one shrug. A calendar is not a designed object; it is a pile of things people happened to call months, kept because nobody stopped.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item all six in order — \textquotedblleft{}Januar, Februar, März, April, Mai, Juni\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two that begin with an English y — \textquotedblleft{}Januar, Juni\textquotedblright{}
  \item the one that ends on a ts — \textquotedblleft{}März\textquotedblright{}
  \item the unit and its cousin — \textquotedblleft{}der Monat, der Mond\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Januar, Februar, März, April, Mai, Juni.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say the first six months. (\textbf{Januar, Februar, März, April, Mai, Juni}.) Which word for the span is German's own? (\emph{\textbf{Der Monat}}, from \emph{Mond}.) Which month shares a god with \emph{Dienstag}? (\emph{\textbf{März}}.) Which one is named for a festival? (\emph{\textbf{Februar}}.) Which one nobody can explain? (\emph{\textbf{April}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
